This is a trigonometric equation counting problem. The goal is to find the number of real solutions in [-pi, pi]. The key idea is to set y = cos^2 x, reduce the equation to a cubic polynomial in y, then count the possible x-values for each valid y.

[Plan]
P1. Set y = cos^2 x and express every term using y.
P2. Simplify the resulting equation to a polynomial in y.
P3. Find all valid roots y in [0, 1].
P4. Count the number of x in [-pi, pi] corresponding to each valid y.
P5. Add the counts to get the total number of solutions.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let y = cos^2 x. Since -pi <= x <= pi, we have y in [0, 1].
S2. [derive] Use the identities cos 4x = 8y^2 - 8y + 1, cos^2 3x = y(4y - 3)^2, cos^3 2x = (2y - 1)^3, and cos^4 x = y^2.
S3. [symbolic] Substitute these into the equation and simplify -> {{(8y^2 - 8y + 1) + y(4y - 3)^2 + (2y - 1)^3 + y^2 => 24y^3 - 27y^2 + 7y}}
S4. [symbolic] Factor the polynomial -> {{24y^3 - 27y^2 + 7y => y(24y^2 - 27y + 7)}}
S5. [calc] Compute the discriminant of the quadratic factor -> <<27^2 - 4*24*7=57>>
S6. [derive] The roots are y = 0 and y = (27 +/- sqrt(57))/48.
S7. [derive] Both nonzero roots lie in (0, 1), since 0 < 27 - sqrt(57) and 27 + sqrt(57) < 48.
S8. [case] For y = 0, cos^2 x = 0 gives x = -pi/2 and x = pi/2, so there are 2 solutions.
S9. [theorem] For each y with 0 < y < 1, the equation cos^2 x = y has exactly 4 solutions in [-pi, pi].
S10. [calc] The two valid nonzero y-values each contribute 4 solutions, so the total is -> <<2+4+4=10>>

[Check]
V1. At y = 0, x = pi/2 gives cos(2pi) + 0 + (-1)^3 + 0 = 1 - 1 = 0.
V2. The quadratic roots y = (27 +/- sqrt(57))/48 are both strictly between 0 and 1, so each gives exactly four x-values.
V3. The total 2 + 4 + 4 = 10 matches all cases.

[Answer]
\boxed{10}

This is a trigonometric quadratic inequality problem. The goal is to find all angles theta for which a certain quadratic in x is strictly positive on the whole interval 0 <= x <= 1. The key idea is to use endpoint conditions and then impose positivity of the quadratic minimum.

[Plan]
P1. Write the expression as a quadratic in x with coefficients depending on sin theta and cos theta.
P2. Use the endpoint values at x = 0 and x = 1 to restrict theta.
P3. Locate the vertex of the quadratic and confirm it lies in the interval 0 <= x <= 1.
P4. Require the minimum value to be positive.
P5. Solve the resulting trigonometric inequality and verify endpoint behavior.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let c = cos theta and s = sin theta, and define Q(x) = c x^2 - x(1-x) + (1-x)^2 s.
S2. [derive] Evaluating at x = 0 gives Q(0) = s > 0, and at x = 1 gives Q(1) = c > 0. Hence theta must lie in the open first quadrant, so 0 < theta < pi/2.
S3. [symbolic] Expand Q(x) -> {{c x^2 - x(1-x) + (1-x)^2 s => (1+c+s)x^2 - (1+2s)x + s}}.
S4. [derive] Let A = 1+c+s and B = 1+2s, so Q(x) = A x^2 - B x + s. Since theta is in the first quadrant, A > 0, and the vertex x0 = B/(2A) satisfies 0 < x0 < 1.
S5. [symbolic] The minimum value on 0 <= x <= 1 is at x0 and equals s - B^2/(4A) -> {{s - (1+2s)^2/(4(1+c+s)) => (4cs-1)/(4(1+c+s))}}.
S6. [derive] Because the denominator 4(1+c+s) is positive, Q(x) > 0 for all 0 <= x <= 1 exactly when 4cs - 1 > 0.
S7. [derive] Since 4cs = 2 sin(2 theta), the condition becomes sin(2 theta) > 1/2. With 0 < theta < pi/2, this gives pi/6 < 2 theta < 5 pi/6, so pi/12 < theta < 5 pi/12.

[Check]
V1. At theta = pi/12, we have sin(2 theta) = 1/2, so the minimum value is 0, which violates the strict inequality.
V2. At theta = pi/4, we have 4 cos theta sin theta = 2 > 1, so the minimum is positive and the endpoints are positive, confirming the condition.

[Answer]
\boxed{(\pi/12,5\pi/12)}

S3. [derive] Since q(x)=\prod_{k=1}^3 (x-a_k), we have \prod_{k=1}^3 (3+a_k) = -q(-3).

S6. [derive] Also 2-sin^2(k*pi/7) = (3+a_k)/2, so the three-factor product is (1/8)*(169/8)=169/64.
S7. [calc] Take the positive square root -> <<sqrt(169/64)=13/8>>

This is a geometry optimization problem involving a triangle with two fixed side lengths. The goal is to maximize tan A. The key idea is to place A and B on the x-axis, express BC=15 as a circle for C, and maximize the slope of AC, whose maximum occurs at a tangent line from A to the circle.

[Plan]
P1. Set coordinates with A at the origin and B on the positive x-axis.
P2. Write the condition BC=15 as a circle for C.
P3. Express tan A as the slope of line AC.
P4. Find the maximum slope by using the tangent from A to the circle.
P5. Solve for the slope and verify the result.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let A=(0,0), B=(20,0), and take C=(x,y) in the upper half-plane so y>0. The condition BC=15 gives (x-20)^2+y^2=225.
S2. [derive] The angle A is the angle between AB and AC, so tan A=y/x. On the circle, x ranges from 5 to 35, so x>0 and tan A is the slope of AC.
S3. [derive] A line through A with slope m has equation y=mx. For C to lie on the circle, this line must meet the circle. The largest possible slope occurs when the line is tangent to the circle.
S4. [derive] The tangent condition means the distance from the center (20,0) to the line mx-y=0 equals the radius 15: 20m/sqrt(m^2+1)=15, with m>0.
S5. [symbolic] Square both sides and simplify -> {{400m^2 = 225(m^2+1) => m^2 = 9/7}}
S6. [calc] Take the positive square root -> <<sqrt(9/7)=3/sqrt(7)>>
S7. [symbolic] Rationalize the denominator -> {{3/sqrt(7) => 3*sqrt(7)/7}}

[Answer]
\boxed{\frac{3\sqrt{7}}{7}}

[Overview]
This is a vector locus problem involving an Apollonius circle or sphere. The goal is to find the center of the fixed-distance locus as a linear combination of a and b. The key idea is to square the distance equation and complete the square.

[Plan]
P1. Square both sides of the distance equation and expand using dot products.
P2. Collect all p terms and complete the square in p.
P3. Identify the center of the resulting circle or sphere.
P4. Express that center as t a + u b and read off t and u.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let c be the fixed center and use the identity ||x-y||^2 = ||x||^2 - 2 x \cdot y + ||y||^2.
S2. [derive] The condition is ||p-b||^2 = 4||p-a||^2.
S3. [symbolic] Expand and move all terms to one side -> {{||p-b||^2 - 4||p-a||^2 = 0 => -3||p||^2 + 2p \cdot (4a-b) + ||b||^2 - 4||a||^2 = 0}}
S4. [symbolic] Divide by -3 and isolate the quadratic p terms -> {{||p||^2 - (2/3)p \cdot (4a-b) + (4||a||^2 - ||b||^2)/3 = 0}}
S5. [symbolic] Complete the square with center c = (4a-b)/3 -> {{||p - (4a-b)/3||^2 = R^2}}
S6. [derive] The center is c = (4/3)a + (-1/3)b, so t = 4/3 and u = -1/3.

[Check]
V1. In the completed square, the linear term is -2p \cdot c. Comparing with -(2/3)p \cdot (4a-b) gives c = (4a-b)/3.
V2. Thus c = (4/3)a + (-1/3)b, so the ordered pair is (4/3,-1/3).

[Answer]
\boxed{(4/3,-1/3)}

[Overview]
This is a trigonometric identity problem. The goal is to find m+n from csc x + cot x = m/n in lowest terms, given sec x + tan x = 22/7. The key idea is to express both expressions in terms of t = tan(x/2).

[Plan]
P1. Introduce t = tan(x/2).
P2. Express sec x + tan x in terms of t.
P3. Use the given value to solve for t.
P4. Express csc x + cot x in terms of t.
P5. Compute the reduced fraction m/n and then m+n.
P6. Verify the result by substituting back.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let t = tan(x/2).
S2. [theorem] Use sin x = 2t/(1+t^2) and cos x = (1-t^2)/(1+t^2).
S3. [symbolic] Simplify sec x + tan x in terms of t -> {{(1+sin x)/cos x => (1+t)/(1-t)}}
S4. [derive] Use the given value to write (1+t)/(1-t) = 22/7.
S5. [symbolic] Solve the equation for t -> {{(1+t)/(1-t)=22/7 => t=15/29}}
S6. [theorem] Use csc x + cot x = (1+cos x)/sin x = 1/t.
S7. [calc] Compute the fraction m/n -> <<1/(15/29)=29/15>>
S8. [calc] Since 29/15 is in lowest terms, compute m+n -> <<29+15=44>>

[Check]
V1. Substitute t = 15/29 into sec x + tan x -> <<(1+15/29)/(1-15/29)=22/7>>
V2. The fraction 29/15 is reduced because gcd(29,15)=1, so m+n=44 is consistent.

[Answer]
\boxed{44}

This is a trigonometric algebra problem. The goal is to express the second product in the form m/n - sqrt(k), then find k+m+n. The key idea is to set x=sin t and y=cos t and use symmetric sums.

[Plan]
P1. Set x=sin t and y=cos t and translate the first condition into equations.
P2. Introduce s=x+y and p=xy, then use x^2+y^2=1.
P3. Solve for s and reject the impossible value.
P4. Compute the second product using s and p.
P5. Identify m, n, k and compute k+m+n.
P6. Verify the resulting expression.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let x=sin t and y=cos t. Then x^2+y^2=1 and the first equation is (1+x)(1+y)=5/4.
S2. [symbolic] Expand the first equation -> {{1+x+y+xy=5/4 => x+y+xy=1/4}}
S3. [setup] Let s=x+y and p=xy. Then s+p=1/4 and x^2+y^2=s^2-2p=1.
S4. [symbolic] Substitute p=1/4-s into x^2+y^2=1 -> {{s^2-2(1/4-s)=1 => s^2+2s-3/2=0}}
S5. [derive] Solving s^2+2s-3/2=0 gives s=-1 +/- sqrt(10)/2.
S6. [case] Since s=x+y and x^2+y^2=1, we have -sqrt(2) <= s <= sqrt(2). The value -1-sqrt(10)/2 is too small, so s=-1+sqrt(10)/2.
S7. [symbolic] Compute p from p=1/4-s -> {{p=1/4-(-1+sqrt(10)/2) => p=5/4-sqrt(10)/2}}
S8. [symbolic] Compute the second product Q=(1-x)(1-y) -> {{Q=1-(x+y)+xy => Q=1-s+p}}
S9. [symbolic] Substitute s and p into Q -> {{Q=1-(-1+sqrt(10)/2)+(5/4-sqrt(10)/2) => Q=13/4-sqrt(10)}}
S10. [derive] Thus m=13, n=4, and k=10.
S11. [calc] Compute k+m+n -> <<10+13+4=27>>

[Check]
V1. The chosen s satisfies s^2+2s-3/2=0 and s+p=1/4 by construction.
V2. These identities imply x^2+y^2=1 and x+y+xy=1/4, so (1+x)(1+y)=5/4.
V3. The second product is Q=13/4-sqrt(10), matching m/n - sqrt(k) with m=13, n=4, k=10.

[Answer]
\boxed{27}

This is a trigonometric summation problem. The goal is to compute floor(100x), where x is the ratio of two finite sums of sine and cosine values. The key idea is to use the standard sum formulas so the common factor cancels, leaving cot(22.5 degrees).

[Plan]
P1. Write x using the given finite sums.
P2. Apply the standard formulas for sums of sines and cosines.
P3. Simplify the quotient to a single trigonometric value.
P4. Evaluate that value and compute floor(100x).
P5. Check the result with a numerical approximation.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let A = sum_{n=1}^{44} cos(n degrees) and B = sum_{n=1}^{44} sin(n degrees), so x = A/B.
S2. [theorem] For theta in degrees, sum_{n=1}^{N} sin(n theta) = sin(N theta/2) sin((N+1) theta/2)/sin(theta/2), and sum_{n=1}^{N} cos(n theta) = sin(N theta/2) cos((N+1) theta/2)/sin(theta/2).
S3. [symbolic] Set N=44 and theta=1 degree. Then the common factors cancel -> {{x = [sin(22 degrees) cos(22.5 degrees)/sin(0.5 degree)]/[sin(22 degrees) sin(22.5 degrees)/sin(0.5 degree)] => cot(22.5 degrees)}}
S4. [symbolic] Use the half-angle identity for tangent -> {{cot(22.5 degrees) => sqrt(2)+1}}
S5. [calc] Multiply by 100 and take the floor -> <<floor(100*(sqrt(2)+1))=241>>

[Check]
V1. Approximate sqrt(2) by 1.41421356.
V2. Then x is approximately 2.41421356, so 100x is approximately 241.421356.
V3. This places 100x between 241 and 242, confirming the floor is 241.

\boxed{241}

This is a trigonometric finite-sum problem. The goal is to evaluate the sum of sines, express it as a tangent of a reduced angle fraction m/n, and compute m+n. The key idea is the standard sine-sum formula and complementary-angle identities.

[Plan]
P1. Apply the finite sine-sum formula with step angle 5 degrees and 35 terms.
P2. Simplify the resulting trigonometric expression using complementary angles.
P3. Identify the tangent angle corresponding to the sum.
P4. Use the range condition m/n < 90 and reduce the angle to a fraction.
P5. Compute m+n and verify the fraction is valid.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let theta = 5 degrees and S = sum_{k=1}^{35} sin(k theta).
S2. [theorem] Use the identity sum_{k=1}^{N} sin(k theta) = sin(N theta/2) sin((N+1)theta/2) / sin(theta/2).
S3. [symbolic] Substitute N=35 and theta=5 into the identity -> {{S = \sin(35*5/2) * \sin(36*5/2) / \sin(5/2) => S = \sin(87.5) / \sin(2.5)}}
S4. [symbolic] Use sin(87.5) = cos(2.5) -> {{S = \cos(2.5) / \sin(2.5) => S = \cot(2.5)}}
S5. [theorem] Since cot(x) = tan(90-x), we have S = tan(87.5).
S6. [derive] Because 0 < m/n < 90 and tangent is one-to-one on (0,90), tan(m/n) = tan(87.5) implies m/n = 87.5.
S7. [symbolic] Express 87.5 as a reduced fraction -> {{87.5 = 175/2 => m=175, n=2}}
S8. [calc] Compute m+n -> <<175+2=177>>

[Check]
V1. Reverse-check the key simplification: sin(87.5)/sin(2.5) = cos(2.5)/sin(2.5) = cot(2.5) = tan(87.5).
V2. The fraction 175/2 is reduced, positive, and less than 90, so the conditions are satisfied.

[Answer]
\boxed{177}

This is a logarithmic trigonometric equation problem. The goal is to determine n from the two given log equations. The key idea is to set a = sin x and b = cos x, convert logarithms to product and sum relations, and use a^2 + b^2 = 1.

[Plan]
P1. Define a = sin x and b = cos x, noting the logarithm domain restrictions.
P2. Convert the first logarithmic equation into a product relation.

P4. Use the Pythagorean identity to relate the sum and product.

S2. [derive] From log10(a) + log10(b) = -1, get log10(ab) = -1, so ab = 10^(-1) = 1/10.
S3. [derive] From log10(a + b) = (1/2)(log10 n - 1), exponentiate to get a + b = sqrt(n/10).
S4. [theorem] Since a = sin x and b = cos x, the Pythagorean identity gives a^2 + b^2 = 1.
S5. [symbolic] Expand the square of the sum and substitute known values -> {{(a+b)^2 = a^2 + b^2 + 2ab = 1 + 2*(1/10) => 6/5}}
S6. [derive] Since a + b = sqrt(n/10), squaring gives (a + b)^2 = n/10.
S7. [calc] Equate the two expressions for (a + b)^2 and solve for n -> <<(6/5)*10=12>>

[Check]

V2. This is consistent with a^2 + b^2 + 2ab = 1 + 2(1/10) = 6/5.
V3. Also (a - b)^2 = 6/5 - 4/10 = 4/5 > 0, so positive a and b satisfying the equations exist.

[Answer]
\boxed{12}

solution:
[Overview]
This is a planar geometry problem involving equilateral triangles and a distance sum. The goal is to find the sum of the squared distances from C to the four possible E vertices. The key idea is to use coordinates, find the two possible D vertices from the circle conditions, and generate the two E vertices for each D by rotations of 60 degrees.

[Plan]
P1. Set up coordinates for the equilateral triangle ABC.
P2. Use the conditions |AD| = sqrt(111) and |BD| = sqrt(11) to locate the two possible D vertices.
P3. For each D, express the two possible E vertices as rotations of D by plus or minus 60 degrees.
P4. Sum |CE|^2 over all four choices using a vector identity.
P5. Compute the final numerical value.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let s = sqrt(111). Put A = (0,0), B = (s,0), and C = (s/2, (sqrt(3)s)/2). Let D = (x,y). Since triangle ADE is equilateral, |AD| = s, and the given condition is |BD| = sqrt(11).
S2. [derive] From x^2 + y^2 = s^2 and (x-s)^2 + y^2 = 11, subtract to get -2sx + s^2 = 11 - s^2. With s^2 = 111, this gives x = 211/(2s).
S3. [derive] The two possible D points are symmetric about the x-axis, so D1 + D2 = (2x,0) = (211/s,0).
S4. [derive] For a fixed D, the two equilateral completions are E+ = R60(D) and E- = R-60(D). Since R60 + R-60 is the identity, E+ + E- = D. Thus |C-E+|^2 + |C-E-|^2 = 4s^2 - 2(C dot D).
S5. [derive] Summing over both D1 and D2 gives total = 8s^2 - 2(C dot (D1 + D2)).
S6. [calc] Since C dot (D1 + D2) = (s/2)(211/s) + ((sqrt(3)s)/2)(0) = 211/2, the total is <<8*111 - 2*(211/2) = 677>>.

[Overview]
This is a roots-of-unity and divisibility problem. The goal is to count n with 1 <= n <= 2012 for which some factor in the product is zero. The key idea is that a zero factor forces an n-th root of unity z to satisfy (1+z)^n = -1, and taking absolute values shows z must be a primitive cube root of unity.

[Plan]
P1. Set z = e^{2 pi i k/n} and view the product as running over all n-th roots of unity.
P2. Determine when a factor vanishes by solving (1+z)^n = -1.
P3. Use absolute values to force z to be one of the primitive cube roots of unity.
P4. Translate the resulting angle equation into a congruence condition on n.
P5. Count the integers n in the given range satisfying that congruence.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let z = e^{2 pi i k/n}. As k runs from 0 to n-1, z runs through all n-th roots of unity, so the product is zero exactly when (1+z)^n + 1 = 0 for some n-th root z.
S2. [derive] If (1+z)^n = -1, then taking absolute values gives |1+z|^n = 1. Since n is positive, |1+z| = 1.
S3. [derive] Write z = e^{i theta}. Then |1+z|^2 = (1+z)(1+\bar z) = 2 + 2 cos(theta). Setting |1+z| = 1 gives cos(theta) = -1/2, so z is one of the two primitive cube roots of unity.
S4. [theorem] A product is zero if and only if at least one of its factors is zero.
S5. [case] If z is a primitive cube root of unity, then z is an n-th root of unity exactly when 3 divides n.
S6. [symbolic] For a primitive cube root z, the number 1+z has order 6, so {{(1+z)^n = -1 => n = 3 (mod 6)}}. The other primitive cube root gives the same condition.
S7. [derive] Conversely, if n = 3 (mod 6), then the primitive cube roots are n-th roots of unity and satisfy (1+z)^n = -1, so a factor is zero. Thus the required n are exactly those congruent to 3 modulo 6.
S8. [calc] These n are 3, 9, 15, ..., 2007, and their number is <<(2007-3)/6+1=335>>.

[Check]
V1. For n=3, taking z=e^{2 pi i/3} gives 1+z=e^{i pi/3}, so (1+z)^3=-1 and the factor is zero.
V2. For n=6, a primitive cube root z has (1+z)^6=1, so (1+z)^6+1=2, not zero, matching the exclusion of even multiples of 3.
V3. The sequence 3,9,...,2007 has common difference 6 and count (2007-3)/6+1=335, which matches the calculation.

[Answer]
\boxed{335}

[Overview]
This is a geometry and trigonometry product problem. The goal is to find the product of twelve chord lengths from the endpoints of a semicircle to six equally spaced interior arc points. The key idea is to express each chord using the central angle and the chord length formula, pair the two chords ending at each C_i, and use a standard sine product identity.

[Plan]
P1. Place the semicircle on a unit circle with central angles and identify the angles of A, B, and each C_i.
P2. Express each chord length AC_i and BC_i using the chord length formula.
P3. Pair AC_i with BC_i and simplify the product of each pair.
P4. Multiply the six paired products and apply the sine product identity.
P5. Simplify the final expression.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let the semicircle have radius 2, with A at angle 0 and B at angle pi. Put C_i at angle i*pi/7 for i = 1,2,...,6.
S2. [theorem] The chord length between two points at central angles u and v is 4*sin(|v-u|/2) here, since the radius is 2 and all relevant central angle differences lie in [0,pi].
S3. [derive] Thus AC_i = 4*sin(i*pi/14), and BC_i = 4*sin((7-i)*pi/14) = 4*cos(i*pi/14).
S4. [symbolic] Simplify each paired product -> {{(4*sin(i*pi/14))*(4*cos(i*pi/14)) => 8*sin(i*pi/7)}}
S5. [derive] Therefore the full product is P = product_{i=1}^{6} 8*sin(i*pi/7) = 8^6 * product_{i=1}^{6} sin(i*pi/7).
S6. [theorem] For n = 7, the identity product_{k=1}^{n-1} sin(k*pi/n) = n/2^(n-1) gives product_{i=1}^{6} sin(i*pi/7) = 7/64.
S7. [calc] Multiply the factors -> <<8^6 * 7/64 = 28672>>

[Check]
V1. Substituting the sine product back gives 8^6 * (7/64) = 262144 * 7/64 = 28672.
V2. The answer is positive and consistent with the magnitudes of the chord lengths involved.

[Answer]
\boxed{28672}

[Plan]

P6. Verify by reversing the recurrence calculation.

S1. [setup] Let \(z_n=a_n+i b_n\). Then the recurrence becomes \(z_{n+1}=(\sqrt{3}+i)z_n\).
S2. [derive] Applying the recurrence 99 times gives \(z_{100}=(\sqrt{3}+i)^{99}z_1\).
S3. [symbolic] Convert \(\sqrt{3}+i\) to polar form -> {{\sqrt(3)+i => 2 e^{i pi/6}}}
S4. [calc] Compute the exponent of the 99th power -> <<99*pi/6=33*pi/2>>
S5. [symbolic] Reduce the phase modulo \(2\pi\) -> {{e^{i*33*pi/2} => i}}
S6. [calc] Compute the 99th power of \(\sqrt{3}+i\) -> <<(sqrt(3)+i)^99=2^99*i>>
S7. [calc] Solve for \(z_1=z_{100}/(\sqrt{3}+i)^{99}\) -> <<(2+4*i)/(2^99*i)=(4-2*i)/2^99>>
S8. [calc] Add the real and imaginary parts of \(z_1\) -> <<4/2^99-2/2^99=1/2^98>>
S9. [symbolic] Write the final value in exponential notation -> {{1/2^98 => 2^{-98}}}

[Check]
V1. Reverse the calculation: \((\sqrt{3}+i)^{99}(4-2i)/2^{99}=i(4-2i)=2+4i\), so \(z_{100}=2+4i\).
V2. The computed real and imaginary parts are \(a_1=4/2^{99}\) and \(b_1=-2/2^{99}\), whose sum is \(2/2^{99}=2^{-98}\).

[Answer]

[Overview]
This is a locus and area problem. The goal is to find the coefficient \(c\) in the area formula for the curve traced by the highest points of the projectile paths as \(\theta\) varies. The key idea is to compute the apex coordinates as functions of \(\theta\), eliminate \(\theta\), and identify the resulting ellipse.

[Plan]
P1. Find the time at which the projectile reaches its highest point.
P2. Substitute this time into the parametric equations to get the apex coordinates.
P3. Eliminate \(\theta\) from the apex coordinates to obtain the locus equation.
P4. Identify the resulting closed curve as an ellipse.
P5. Compute its area, including the scale factor \(v^2/g\), and determine \(c\).

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let the apex coordinates be \((x_h,y_h)\), and define scaled coordinates
\[
X=\frac{x_h g}{v^2},\qquad Y=\frac{y_h g}{v^2}.
\]
S2. [derive] The vertical velocity is \(v\sin\theta-gt\). At the highest point,
\[
v\sin\theta-gt=0,
\]
so
\[
t_h=\frac{v\sin\theta}{g}.
\]
S3. [derive] Substituting \(t_h\) into the parametric equations gives
\[
x_h=\frac{v^2}{g}\sin\theta\cos\theta,
\qquad
y_h=\frac{v^2}{2g}\sin^2\theta.
\]
S4. [symbolic] In scaled coordinates, \(X=\sin\theta\cos\theta\) and \(Y=\frac12\sin^2\theta\). Since \(\sin^2\theta=2Y\), eliminating \(\theta\) gives
\[
X^2=2Y(1-2Y).
\]
Thus
\[
{{X^2=2Y(1-2Y) => X^2+4\left(Y-\frac14\right)^2=\frac14}}.
\]
S5. [theorem] This is an ellipse centered at \(\left(0,\frac14\right)\) with horizontal semiaxis \(\frac12\) and vertical semiaxis \(\frac14\).
S6. [calc] The area in scaled coordinates is
\[
<<\pi\left(\frac12\right)\left(\frac14\right)=\frac{\pi}{8}>>.
\]
S7. [calc] The original coordinates are obtained by multiplying by \(v^2/g\) in both directions, so the area is multiplied by \((v^2/g)^2\):
\[
<<\frac{\pi}{8}\left(\frac{v^2}{g}\right)^2=\frac{\pi}{8}\cdot\frac{v^4}{g^2}>>.
\]

[Check]
V1. At \(\theta=0\), the apex is \((0,0)\); at \(\theta=90^\circ\), it is \((0,v^2/(2g))\); at \(\theta=45^\circ\), it is \((v^2/(2g),v^2/(4g))\). These match the ellipse extrema.
V2. The ellipse has semiaxes \(v^2/(2g)\) and \(v^2/(4g)\), so its area is \(\pi(v^2/(2g))(v^2/(4g))=\pi v^4/(8g^2)\), giving \(c=\pi/8\).

[Answer]
\boxed{\frac{\pi}{8}}

[Overview]
This is a polynomial-root and cotangent-addition problem. The goal is to compute the cotangent of a sum of arccotangents of all roots. The key idea is to encode each arccotangent through the quotient (z+i)/(z-i), multiply over all roots, and evaluate the resulting polynomial at i and -i.

[Plan]
P1. Define the polynomial and the arccotangent variables.
P2. Derive a product formula for the exponential of twice the sum.
P3. Use the even degree factorization to rewrite the product as P(-i)/P(i).
P4. Evaluate P(i) from the coefficient pattern.
P5. Convert the product back to cotangent and simplify.
P6. Check the arithmetic and sign.

[Solution]

[Overview]
This is a trigonometric sequence problem. The goal is to find the least positive real value of t for which four arcsin-sine values can form a geometric progression for some \alpha in (0,\pi/2). The key idea is to use the first three terms to determine the possible common ratios, then choose the smallest t that realizes the fourth term.

[Plan]
P1. Define the four terms and use the geometric progression condition on the first three terms.
P2. Split the interval for \alpha according to the formula for \arcsin(\sin 2\alpha).
P3. Solve the resulting equations for possible \alpha.
P4. Compute the common ratio r for each valid \alpha and determine the least t from the fourth term.
P5. Compare the candidates and verify the least value.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let a_k=\arcsin(\sin(k\alpha)) for k=1,2,7,t. Since 0<\alpha<\pi/2, we have a_1=\alpha. If a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4 is a GP with ratio r, then r=a_2/a_1>0 and a_4=a_1r^3.

S2. [case] If 0<\alpha<\pi/4, then a_2=2\alpha, so r=2. The condition a_3=a_1r^2 becomes \arcsin(\sin 7\alpha)=4\alpha. Since the right side is at most \pi/2, \alpha\le\pi/8. In this range the equation gives \alpha=\pi/11. Then a_4=a_1r^3=8\pi/11>\pi/2, impossible because every arcsin value is at most \pi/2. So this case gives no four-term GP.

S3. [case] If \alpha=\pi/4, then a_2=\pi/2 and r=2, so a_3 would equal \pi, impossible. Thus \alpha\ne\pi/4.

S4. [case] If \pi/4<\alpha<\pi/2, then a_2=\pi-2\alpha. Write x=\alpha/\pi, so 1/4<x<1/2. The GP condition is
a_3=\frac{a_2^2}{a_1}=\pi\frac{(1-2x)^2}{x}.
Let h(x)=\frac{(1-2x)^2}{x}. Since a_3\le\pi/2, we need h(x)\le1/2.

S5. [derive] In the allowed range, the equation a_3=\arcsin(\sin 7\alpha) becomes \pi h(x)=\arcsin(\sin 7\pi x). The possible congruences are 7x=2+h(x) and 7x=3-h(x). Solving h(x)=7x-2 gives x=1/3. Solving h(x)=3-7x gives 11x^2-7x+1=0, so x=(7+\sqrt5)/22 or x=(7-\sqrt5)/22; only x=(7+\sqrt5)/22 lies in the allowed interval.

S6. [symbolic] For x=(7+\sqrt5)/22, compute the common ratio -> {{r = (1-2x)/x => (3-\sqrt5)/2}}

S7. [symbolic] The least t for this \alpha is r^3, so cube the ratio -> {{((3-\sqrt5)/2)^3 => 9-4\sqrt5}}

S8. [derive] For any valid GP, the fourth term is a_1r^3. Since 0<a_4\le\pi/2, the smallest positive t satisfying \arcsin(\sin(t\alpha))=a_4 is t=a_4/\alpha=r^3. The possible ratios are r=2 for \alpha=\pi/11, which gives no fourth term; r=1 for \alpha=\pi/3, giving t=1; and r=(3-\sqrt5)/2, giving t=9-4\sqrt5. Since 9-4\sqrt5<1, the least value is attained at \alpha=\pi(7+\sqrt5)/22.

[Check]
V1. For \alpha=\pi(7+\sqrt5)/22 and t=9-4\sqrt5, the first three terms have common ratio r=(3-\sqrt5)/2 by construction.
V2. The fourth term equals a_1r^3=t\alpha, and since 0<t\alpha<\pi/2, \arcsin(\sin(t\alpha))=t\alpha. Thus the four terms form a GP.
V3. The numerical value is t=9-4\sqrt5\approx0.055728, which is smaller than the other realizable candidate t=1.

[Answer]
\boxed{9-4\sqrt{5}}

[Overview]
This is a trigonometric identifiability problem. The goal is to find all possible values on Malvina's card that allow her, after all three values are shared, to uniquely determine the function while the other two students cannot. The key idea is to analyze when the multiset {sin x, cos x, tan x} determines the function assignment uniquely and when a repeated value creates ambiguity.

[Plan]
P1. Set s = sin x, c = cos x, and t = tan x, so the students know the multiset {s,c,t}.
P2. Determine when the multiset allows more than one function assignment for a given value.
P3. Analyze the cases where exactly one student can identify her function.
P4. Collect all possible identifiable values on Malvina's card and sum them.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let s = sin x, c = cos x, and t = tan x = s/c, where 0 < x < 90 degrees. After sharing, every student knows the multiset {s,c,t} and her own value.
S2. [derive] If s,c,t are pairwise distinct, checking the possible reassignments of which value is tan y for another acute angle y shows that the only new multiset would require t = c, giving a repeated value. Thus, with distinct values, the multiset determines x and the function assignment, so all three students could identify their functions.
S3. [case] Repeated values occur only when s = c, or when t = c. The equality s = t would imply c = 1, impossible for acute x.
S4. [derive] If s = c, then x = 45 degrees, with s = c = sqrt(2)/2 and t = 1. The multiset is {sqrt(2)/2, sqrt(2)/2, 1}. The holder of 1 can identify it as tan, while the two holders of sqrt(2)/2 cannot distinguish sin from cos.
S5. [derive] If t = c, then s/c = c, so s = c^2. Since s^2 + c^2 = 1, we get s^2 + s - 1 = 0, hence s = (sqrt(5) - 1)/2. The multiset is {s,c,c}. The holder of s can identify it as sin, while the two holders of c cannot distinguish cos from tan.
S6. [case] In both repeated-value cases, exactly one value has a unique function assignment: 1 in the first case and (sqrt(5) - 1)/2 in the second case.
S7. [derive] Therefore, the only possible values on Malvina's card are 1 and (sqrt(5) - 1)/2.
S8. [calc] Sum the possible values -> <<1+(sqrt(5)-1)/2=(sqrt(5)+1)/2>>.

[Check]
V1. For x = 45 degrees, the multiset {sqrt(2)/2, sqrt(2)/2, 1} lets only the holder of 1 identify the function, namely tan.
V2. For the other case, s = (sqrt(5) - 1)/2 satisfies s^2 + s - 1 = 0, giving t = c and multiset {s,c,c}; only s is uniquely identifiable, as sin.
V3. The sum 1 + (sqrt(5) - 1)/2 equals (sqrt(5) + 1)/2, consistent with the calculation.

[Answer]
\boxed{\frac{\sqrt5+1}{2}}

[Overview]
This is a triangle area-ratio problem. The goal is to compute [PQR]/[ABC] for the small triangle formed by three cevians. The key idea is to use affine invariance to place the triangle at convenient coordinates, find the three intersection points, and compute the area ratio.

[Plan]
P1. Choose convenient coordinates for triangle ABC using affine invariance.
P2. Determine the coordinates of D, E, and F from the given ratios.
P3. Find equations for lines AD, BE, and CF.
P4. Compute the intersections P, Q, and R.
P5. Calculate the area of triangle PQR and divide by the area of ABC.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] By affine invariance, set A=(0,0), B=(1,0), and C=(0,1). Then [ABC]=1/2.
S2. [derive] From BD:DC=1:2, D=(2/3,1/3); from CE:EA=1:2, E=(0,2/3); from AF:FB=1:2, F=(1/3,0).
S3. [derive] The cevians have equations AD: y=x/2, BE: 2x+3y=2, and CF: 3x+y=1.
S4. [derive] Solving the line intersections gives P=(2/7,1/7), Q=(4/7,2/7), and R=(1/7,4/7).
S5. [calc] Twice the area of PQR is the absolute determinant of Q-P and R-P -> <<abs((4/7-2/7)*(4/7-1/7)-(2/7-1/7)*(1/7-2/7))=1/7>>
S6. [derive] Since twice the area of PQR is 1/7, [PQR]=1/14.
S7. [calc] Compute the desired ratio -> <<(1/14)/(1/2)=1/7>>

[Check]
V1. Routh theorem with ratios x=y=z=1/2 gives ((xyz-1)^2)/((xy+x+1)(yz+y+1)(zx+z+1))=1/7, agreeing.
V2. The value 1/7 lies between 0 and 1, as required for an area ratio.

[Answer]
\boxed{\frac{1}{7}}

[Overview]
This is a vector projection geometry problem. The goal is to find a vector v=(v1,v2) with v1+v2=2 for which the projection of BA equals PA. The key idea is that both given lines have direction (4,3), so PA is along the normal vector (3,-4), and v must be a scalar multiple of that normal vector.

[Plan]
P1. Identify the common direction vector of the two lines.
P2. Choose a normal vector to line m.
P3. Use the perpendicular foot condition to relate PA to the normal component of BA.
P4. Write v as a scalar multiple of the normal vector.

P6. Verify the result using a sample point.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] The common direction is d=(4,3), and a normal vector is n=(3,-4). Let v=lambda*n for some nonzero scalar lambda.
S2. [theorem] The vector projection of BA onto any nonzero scalar multiple of n equals the projection of BA onto n.
S3. [derive] Since B lies on m and P is the foot from A to m, the component of BA in the n direction is exactly PA. Thus PA is the projection of BA onto v=lambda*n.
S4. [calc] The coordinate sum of n is <<3+(-4)=-1>>.
S5. [symbolic] The condition v1+v2=2 gives {{lambda*(3+(-4))=2 => lambda=-2}}.
S6. [calc] Therefore v=lambda*n is <<(-2*3, -2*(-4))=(-6,8)>>.

[Check]
V1. v=(-6,8) is parallel to n=(3,-4) because v=-2n, and its coordinate sum is <<-6+8=2>>.
V2. For A=(1,4) and B=(-5,6), BA=(6,-2). The projection onto v=(-6,8) is (78/25,-104/25).
V3. The foot P of A on m is (-53/25,204/25), so PA=(78/25,-104/25), matching V2.

\boxed{\begin{pmatrix}-6\\8\end{pmatrix}}

[Overview]
This is a solid geometry volume problem. The goal is to find the larger volume after a cube is cut by a plane through a vertex and two edge midpoints. The key idea is to assign coordinates, find the cutting plane, and integrate the smaller piece's height over its base.

[Plan]
P1. Assign standard coordinates to the cube and locate D, M, and N.
P2. Find the equation of the cutting plane through D, M, and N.
P3. Identify the side with smaller volume using the plane equation.
P4. Express the smaller volume as an integral over its base in the xy-plane.
P5. Subtract the smaller volume from 1 to get the larger volume.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let A=(0,0,0), B=(1,0,0), C=(1,1,0), D=(0,1,0), E=(0,0,1), F=(1,0,1), G=(1,1,1), H=(0,1,1). Then M=(1/2,0,0) and N=(1,1,1/2).

S2. [derive] The plane through D, M, and N has equation 2x+y-4z=1.

S3. [derive] The smaller solid lies on the side containing B and C, where 2x+y-4z-1>=0. Thus z <= (2x+y-1)/4. This height is positive exactly when 2x+y>1.

S4. [setup] Let R be the region in the unit square 0<=x<=1, 0<=y<=1 with 2x+y>=1. The smaller volume is V_small=(1/4) times the integral over R of (2x+y-1) dA.

S5. [derive] Over the full unit square, the integral of 2x+y-1 is 1/2. The excluded triangular region T has vertices (0,0), (0,1), (1/2,0), and the integral of 2x+y-1 over T is the area times the average vertex value.

S6. [calc] Evaluate the excluded integral -> <<(1/4)*((-1+0+0)/3)=-1/12>>.

S7. [calc] Subtract the excluded integral from the full-square integral -> <<1/2-(-1/12)=7/12>>.

S8. [calc] Compute the smaller volume -> <<(1/4)*(7/12)=7/48>>.

S9. [calc] Compute the larger volume -> <<1-7/48=41/48>>.

[Check]
V1. The two volumes sum to the cube volume -> <<7/48+41/48=1>>.
V2. Since 41/48>7/48, the larger solid has volume 41/48.

[Answer]
\boxed{\frac{41}{48}}

S2. [theorem] In any triangle, a larger side is opposite a larger angle, so the doubled angle must be opposite the side of length 15.
S3. [derive] By the Law of Sines, 15/sin(2B) = 9/sin(B).
S4. [symbolic] Use the identity sin(2B) = 2 sin(B) cos(B) and sin(B) != 0: {{15/(sin(B)*(2cos(B))) = 9/sin(B) => 15 = 18 cos(B)}}.
S5. [calc] From 15 = 18 cos(B), get cos(B) = 5/6, so sin^2(B) = 1 - cos^2(B): <<1-(5/6)^2=11/36>>.
S6. [derive] Since A + B + C = 180 and A = 2B, the third angle is C = 180 - 3B, so sin(C) = sin(3B).

[Answer]

[Overview]
This is a transcendental equation counting problem. The goal is to count intersections of sin x with the positive decreasing exponential 2^(-x) on (0,100pi). The key idea is to split the interval into positive sine humps and use monotonicity and concavity to count one crossing on each side of every hump.

[Plan]
P1. Identify where sin x is positive on (0,100pi).
P2. Define f(x) = sin x - 2^(-x) and count roots on rising halves of the sine humps.
P3. Count roots on falling halves using a shifted cosine-exponential difference.
P4. Multiply the number of positive humps by the number of roots per hump.
P5. Check the interval endpoints and the total count.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Define f(x) = sin x - 2^(-x). Since 2^(-x) > 0, solutions require sin x > 0.
S2. [derive] On (0,100pi), the positive sine intervals are (2k pi, (2k+1)pi) for k = 0,1,...,49, giving 50 positive half-periods.
S3. [derive] On each rising half (2k pi, 2k pi + pi/2), we have f(2k pi) = -2^(-2k pi) < 0 and f(2k pi + pi/2) = 1 - 2^(-(2k pi + pi/2)) > 0. Also f'(x) = cos x + (ln 2)2^(-x) > 0 there, so f is strictly increasing and has exactly one zero on each rising half.
S4. [case] On each falling half, write x = 2k pi + pi/2 + t with 0 < t < pi/2, and define h(t) = cos t - C_k 2^(-t), where C_k = 2^(-(2k pi + pi/2)).
S5. [derive] For h(t), h(0) = 1 - C_k > 0 and h(pi/2) = -C_k 2^(-pi/2) < 0. Also h''(t) = -cos t - C_k (ln 2)^2 2^(-t) < 0, so h is strictly concave. Moreover h'(0) = C_k ln 2 > 0 and h'(pi/2) < 0, so h increases then decreases and crosses zero exactly once on (0,pi/2).
S6. [calc] Each of the 50 positive half-periods contributes exactly 2 roots, so total = <<50*2=100>>.

[Check]
V1. The last positive half-period has k = 49 and is (98pi,99pi), which lies inside (0,100pi); the next positive half-period would start at 100pi and is excluded, confirming 50 positive half-periods.
V2. On each positive half-period, f is negative at the left zero of sine, positive at the sine peak, and negative again at the right zero of sine, consistent with exactly one crossing on each side of the peak.

[Answer]
\boxed{100}

[Overview]
This is a trigonometric optimization problem. The goal is to find the minimum value of a rational expression in sin x and cos x. The key idea is to set s = sin^2 x and c = cos^2 x, reducing the expression to a one-variable function of p = sc.

[Plan]
P1. Introduce s = sin^2 x and c = cos^2 x with s + c = 1.
P2. Express sin^6 x + cos^6 x and sin^4 x + cos^4 x in terms of p = sc.
P3. Write the given quotient as a function of p.
P4. Determine the allowed interval for p using s + c = 1.
P5. Use monotonicity to locate the minimum and verify it.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let s = sin^2 x and c = cos^2 x. Then s >= 0, c >= 0, and s + c = 1.
S2. [setup] Let p = sc = sin^2 x cos^2 x.
S3. [symbolic] Compute the sixth-power sum -> {{sin^6 x + cos^6 x = s^3 + c^3 = (s+c)^3 - 3sc(s+c) => 1 - 3p}}
S4. [symbolic] Compute the fourth-power sum -> {{sin^4 x + cos^4 x = s^2 + c^2 = (s+c)^2 - 2sc => 1 - 2p}}
S5. [symbolic] Rewrite the quotient -> {{(sin^6 x + cos^6 x + 1)/(sin^4 x + cos^4 x + 1) = ((1-3p)+1)/((1-2p)+1) => (2-3p)/(2-2p)}}
S6. [derive] Since s + c = 1 and s,c >= 0, the product satisfies 0 <= p = sc <= (s+c)^2/4 = 1/4.
S7. [derive] Let f(p) = (2-3p)/(2-2p). Then f'(p) = -2/(2-2p)^2 < 0, so f is decreasing on [0,1/4].
S8. [calc] The minimum occurs at p = 1/4 and equals <<(2-3*(1/4))/(2-2*(1/4))=5/6>>.
S9. [case] Equality p = 1/4 requires s = c = 1/2, which is attainable when sin^2 x = cos^2 x = 1/2.

[Check]
V1. Substitute p = 1/4 into the reduced function -> <<(2-3/4)/(2-1/2)=5/6>>.
V2. Check the other endpoint p = 0 -> <<(2-0)/(2-0)=1>>, which is greater than 5/6.
V3. Directly at x = pi/4, the numerator is 1/8 + 1/8 + 1 = 5/4 and the denominator is 1/4 + 1/4 + 1 = 3/2, giving (5/4)/(3/2) = 5/6.

[Answer]
\boxed{\frac{5}{6}}

[Overview]
This is a vector geometry problem involving the altitudes of an acute triangle. The goal is to determine angle ACB from a linear relation among the three altitude vectors. The key idea is to place the triangle in coordinates, express each altitude vector in terms of the side ratio and the cosine and sine of angle C, and solve the resulting component equations.

[Plan]
P1. Set coordinates with C at the origin and A on the positive x-axis.
P2. Express B using the side length ratio r = BC/AC and the angle at C.
P3. Compute the three altitude vectors AD, BE, and CF in coordinates.
P4. Use both components of the given vector equation to form equations in r and cos C.
P5. Solve for cos C and then determine angle C.
P6. Check the result by substitution into the original vector equation.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Scale so AC = 1 and place C=(0,0), A=(1,0). Let u=\cos C and v=\sin C, where C = angle ACB. Let BC=r, so B=(r u,r v), with v>0.

S2. [derive] The foot D of A onto line BC is D=(u^2,u v), so
\vec{AD}=(-v^2,u v).
The foot E of B onto CA is E=(r u,0), so
\vec{BE}=(0,-r v).

S3. [derive] Let L^2=AB^2=1+r^2-2r u. Projecting C onto line AB gives the foot F and hence
\vec{CF}=\left(\frac{r^2 v^2}{L^2},\frac{r(1-r u)v}{L^2}\right).

S4. [derive] Substitute into
9\vec{AD}+4\vec{BE}+7\vec{CF}=0.
The x-component gives
-9v^2+\frac{7r^2v^2}{L^2}=0.
The y-component, after dividing by v, gives
9u-4r+\frac{7r(1-r u)}{L^2}=0.

S5. [derive] Since v>0, the x-component yields L^2=\frac{7r^2}{9}. Substituting this into the y-component gives
9u-4r+\frac{9}{r}(1-r u)=0.
The terms 9u and -9u cancel, leaving
-4r+\frac{9}{r}=0.

S6. [derive] Thus 4r^2=9. Because r>0, r=\frac{3}{2}. Then
L^2=\frac{7r^2}{9}=\frac{7}{4}.
Using L^2=1+r^2-2r u gives
\frac{7}{4}=1+\frac{9}{4}-3u,
so u=\frac{1}{2}.

S7. [derive] Since u=\cos C=\frac{1}{2} and C is acute, we have C=60^\circ.

[Check]
V1. For C=60^\circ and r=3/2, we have u=1/2, v=\sqrt{3}/2, and L^2=7/4.
V2. The altitude vectors are \vec{AD}=(-3/4,\sqrt{3}/4), \vec{BE}=(0,-3\sqrt{3}/4), and \vec{CF}=(27/28,3\sqrt{3}/28).
V3. Substitution gives 9\vec{AD}+4\vec{BE}+7\vec{CF}=(0,0), so the original vector equation is satisfied.
V4. The triangle is acute for these values because r u=3/4<1 and u<r, so the altitude feet lie on the corresponding sides.

[Answer]
\boxed{60^\circ}

[Overview]
This is a trigonometric simplification using 13th roots of unity. The goal is to evaluate the sum of three cosines. The key idea is to identify the angles with quadratic residues modulo 13 and use the quadratic Gauss period.

[Plan]
P1. Define the 13th roots of unity and the set of quadratic residues modulo 13.
P2. Pair each residue term with its negative to relate the root-of-unity sum to the given cosine sum.
P3. Use the quadratic Gauss sum for the prime 13 to evaluate the relevant period.
P4. Solve for the required cosine sum and verify the result numerically.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let z = e^{2\pi i/13}. The quadratic residues modulo 13 are QR = {1,3,4,9,10,12}. Define S = \sum_{a \in QR} z^a.
S2. [derive] Since -1 is a quadratic residue modulo 13, the set QR is closed under negation. Therefore the terms pair as z^1 with z^12, z^3 with z^10, and z^4 with z^9, giving S = 2(\cos(2\pi/13) + \cos(6\pi/13) + \cos(8\pi/13)).
S3. [theorem] For an odd prime p, the quadratic Gauss sum satisfies G = \sum_{a=1}^{p-1} (a/p) z^a, and for p = 13, since 13 \equiv 1 \pmod 4, one has G = \sqrt{13}.
S4. [derive] Let T be the sum of z^a over nonresidue exponents modulo 13. Then G = S - T, while S + T = \sum_{a=1}^{12} z^a = -1.
S5. [symbolic] Solve the two equations for S -> {{S - T = \sqrt{13}, S + T = -1 => S = (\sqrt{13}-1)/2}}.
S6. [symbolic] Use S = 2E, where E is the required cosine sum, to solve for E -> {{S = 2E and S = (\sqrt{13}-1)/2 => E = (\sqrt{13}-1)/4}}.

[Check]
V1. Numerically, the original sum is about 0.6514, and (\sqrt{13}-1)/4 is about 0.6514, so the value is consistent.
V2. Multiplying the answer by 2 gives (\sqrt{13}-1)/2, which matches the computed real Gaussian period S.

[Answer]

[Overview]
This is a linear algebra problem about a reflection matrix. The goal is to find R^2, where R reflects vectors across the line spanned by (3,1). The key idea is that reflecting twice across the same line returns every vector to itself, so R^2 is the identity matrix.

[Plan]
P1. Identify the geometric action of reflection across the given line.
P2. Decompose any vector into components parallel and perpendicular to the line.
P3. Apply the reflection twice and observe that the perpendicular sign change cancels.
P4. Conclude that R^2 is the identity matrix.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let L be the line spanned by v = (3,1). For any vector x in R^2, write x = x_parallel + x_perp, where x_parallel is parallel to L and x_perp is perpendicular to L.
S2. [theorem] Reflection across L fixes every vector parallel to L and negates every vector perpendicular to L.
S3. [derive] Applying R once sends x_parallel + x_perp to x_parallel - x_perp.
S4. [derive] Applying R again sends x_parallel - x_perp to x_parallel - (-x_perp) = x_parallel + x_perp = x.
S5. [theorem] Since R^2(x) = x for every vector x in R^2, R^2 is the identity transformation.
S6. [derive] Therefore R^2 is represented by the 2 by 2 identity matrix.

[Check]
V1. The vector (3,1) lies on the reflection line, so it is fixed by R and also fixed by R^2.
V2. A perpendicular vector, for example (-1,3), is negated by R and restored by applying R again.
V3. Since the parallel and perpendicular directions span R^2, R^2 fixes every vector, confirming the identity matrix.

[Answer]
\boxed{\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}}

[Overview]
This is a trigonometric geometry problem. The goal is to find all possible values of x for which an isosceles triangle has equal sides cos x, base cos 7x, and vertex angle 2x. The key idea is to use the law of cosines to get cos 7x = sin 2x, then solve the resulting cosine equation with triangle restrictions.

[Plan]
P1. Set up the equal sides, base, and vertex angle of the isosceles triangle.
P2. Use the law of cosines to relate the base to the equal sides and vertex angle.
P3. Simplify the relation to a trigonometric equation.
P4. Solve the trigonometric equation using general cosine equality.
P5. Restrict the solutions to the valid triangle angle range and verify them.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let the equal sides be a = cos x, the base be b = cos 7x, and the vertex angle between the equal sides be 2x. Since the triangle is nondegenerate, 0 < 2x < 180, so 0 < x < 90.

S2. [theorem] By the law of cosines applied to the two equal sides, b^2 = a^2 + a^2 - 2a^2 cos(2x).

S3. [derive] Since 1 - cos(2x) = 2 sin^2 x, we get b^2 = 4a^2 sin^2 x. Because a > 0 and sin x > 0 on 0 < x < 90, this gives b = 2a sin x.

S4. [derive] Substitute a = cos x and b = cos 7x to obtain cos 7x = 2 cos x sin x = sin 2x. Since sin 2x = cos(90 - 2x), the equation is cos 7x = cos(90 - 2x).

S5. [theorem] For real angles A and B, cos A = cos B exactly when A = B + 360k or A = -B + 360k for some integer k.

S6. [case] Using A = 7x and B = 90 - 2x, the first case is 7x = 90 - 2x + 360k. This gives 9x = 90 + 360k, so x = 10 + 40k. With 0 < x < 90, the valid values are k = 0 and k = 1, giving x = 10 and x = 50.

S7. [case] The second case is 7x = -(90 - 2x) + 360k, so 7x = -90 + 2x + 360k. This gives 5x = -90 + 360k, so x = -18 + 72k. With 0 < x < 90, the only valid value is k = 1, giving x = 54.

S8. [derive] The candidate values are therefore 10, 50, and 54. For each, 0 < x < 90 gives positive equal sides cos x, and cos 7x = sin 2x = 2 cos x sin x > 0. Also 2 cos x sin x < 2 cos x because sin x < 1, so the triangle inequality holds.

[Check]
V1. For x = 10, cos 70 = sin 20 = 2 cos 10 sin 10, so the side and angle relation holds.
V2. For x = 50, cos 350 = cos 10 = sin 80 = sin 100 = 2 cos 50 sin 50, so the relation holds.
V3. For x = 54, cos 378 = cos 18 = sin 72 = sin 108 = 2 cos 54 sin 54, so the relation holds.
V4. All three values satisfy 0 < x < 90 and produce positive side lengths with vertex angles 20, 100, and 108 degrees respectively, so all are valid.

[Answer]
\boxed{10, 50, 54}

S6. [calc] Compute \(\sin^2 q\) -> <<1-144/169=25/169>>
S7. [symbolic] Combine tangent identities -> {{tan x + tan y = sin(2p)/(cos(p+q)cos(p-q)) => tan x + tan y = [2 tan p/(1+tan^2 p)]/[cos^2 p - sin^2 q]}}
S8. [calc] Substitute the values into the formula -> <<(2*(4/3)/(1+16/9))/(9/25-25/169)=507/112>>

[Overview]
This is a trigonometric counting problem. The goal is to compute the sum of F(n) for n from 2 to 2007, where F(n) counts solutions of sin x = sin nx on [0, pi]. The key idea is to use the general sine equality condition, count two families of solutions, subtract overlaps, and then sum the resulting formula.

[Plan]
P1. Translate sin x = sin nx into two congruence families.
P2. Count the solutions from the first family on [0, pi].
P3. Count the solutions from the second family on [0, pi].
P4. Determine when the two families overlap and subtract those duplicated points.
P5. Write a closed formula for F(n).
P6. Sum the formula from n = 2 to 2007 and subtract the overlap correction totals.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] For each n > 1, count the distinct x in [0, pi] satisfying sin x = sin nx.
S2. [derive] Since sin A = sin B exactly when A = B + 2k pi or A = pi - B + 2k pi, the solutions split into x = nx + 2k pi and x = pi - nx + 2k pi for integers k.
S3. [derive] The first family gives x = 2m pi/(n-1) with integer m. The condition 0 <= x <= pi gives 0 <= m <= (n-1)/2, so this family has floor((n-1)/2)+1 = ceil(n/2) solutions.
S4. [derive] The second family gives x = (2k+1) pi/(n+1) with integer k. The condition 0 <= x <= pi gives positive odd integers 2k+1 <= n+1, so this family has floor(n/2)+1 solutions.
S5. [derive] A point can belong to both families only when 2x = pi mod 2pi, so in [0, pi] the only possible common point is x = pi/2. This point is a solution exactly when sin(n pi/2) = 1, which happens exactly when n mod 4 = 1.
S6. [derive] Thus F(n) = ceil(n/2) + floor(n/2) + 1 - d(n), where d(n) = 1 if n mod 4 = 1 and d(n) = 0 otherwise. Since ceil(n/2)+floor(n/2)=n, we get F(n) = n+1-d(n).
S7. [calc] Sum n from 2 to 2007 -> <<(2+2007)*2006/2=2015027>>
S8. [calc] Add the constant 1 over the 2006 terms -> <<2015027+2006=2017033>>
S9. [derive] The integers n in [2, 2007] with n mod 4 = 1 are 5, 9, ..., 2005, and their count is (2005-5)/4+1.
S10. [calc] Count those correction terms -> <<(2005-5)/4+1=501>>
S11. [calc] Subtract the correction from the sum -> <<2017033-501=2016532>>

[Check]
V1. For n = 2, the formula gives F(2) = 3, which matches sin x = sin 2x giving x = 0, pi/3, pi.
V2. For n = 5, the formula gives F(5) = 5 after subtracting the common point x = pi/2, matching a direct family count.
V3. The final sum uses 2006 terms, includes the constant +2006, and subtracts exactly 501 values of n with n mod 4 = 1, so the arithmetic is consistent.

[Answer]
\boxed{2016532}

S8. [derive] For cos a = -1/sqrt(2) in (0,360), a = 135 or a = 225 degrees.

S5. [symbolic] Solve the coefficient equations -> {{ y-1/\sqrt{2}=0, -x-1/\sqrt{2}=0 => y=1/\sqrt{2}, x=-1/\sqrt{2} }}

[Plan]
P1. Set x = sin 50 degrees and write csc 50 degrees as 1/x.
P2. Use sin 150 degrees and the triple-angle formula to obtain a polynomial relation for x.
P3. Show that (3 - 1/x)^2 equals 9 - 8x using that relation.
P4. Verify the positive square root sign and identify a and b.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let x = sin 50 degrees. Then csc 50 degrees = 1/x, and x > 0.
S2. [theorem] Use the triple-angle identity sin(3 theta) = 3 sin theta - 4 sin^3 theta with theta = 50 degrees.
S3. [symbolic] Since sin 150 degrees = 1/2, substitute x -> {{3*x - 4*x^3 = 1/2 => 8*x^3 - 6*x + 1 = 0}}.
S4. [symbolic] Divide the relation by x^2 -> {{(8*x^3 - 6*x + 1)/x^2 = 0 => 1/x^2 = 6/x - 8*x}}.
S5. [symbolic] Expand and substitute this relation -> {{(3 - 1/x)^2 = 9 - 6/x + 1/x^2 = 9 - 6/x + (6/x - 8*x) => 9 - 8*x}}.
S6. [derive] Thus (3 - 1/x)^2 = 9 - 8x, so sqrt(9 - 8x) = |3 - 1/x|.
S7. [derive] Since sin 50 degrees > sin 30 degrees = 1/2, we have 1/x < 2, so 3 - 1/x > 0.
S8. [derive] Therefore sqrt(9 - 8x) = 3 - 1/x.
S9. [derive] Replacing x by sin 50 degrees gives sqrt(9 - 8 sin 50 degrees) = 3 - csc 50 degrees = 3 + (-1)csc 50 degrees.
S10. [derive] Comparing with a + b csc 50 degrees gives a = 3 and b = -1.

[Check]

V3. Since sin 50 degrees > 1/2, we have csc 50 degrees < 2, hence 3 - csc 50 degrees is positive and equals the positive square root.
V4. Therefore the ordered pair is (a,b) = (3,-1).

[Answer]

S1. [setup] Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}2&3\\5&d\end{pmatrix}\) and assume \(A^{-1}=kA\).
S2. [derive] Multiply both sides by \(A\): \(I=kA^2\).
S3. [symbolic] Compute the square of \(A\) -> {{A \cdot A => \begin{pmatrix}19&6+3d\\10+5d&15+d^2\end{pmatrix}}}
S4. [derive] Since \(I\) is a scalar multiple of the identity and \(k\) is nonzero, \(A^2\) must also be a scalar multiple of the identity, so its off-diagonal entries must be zero.
S5. [symbolic] Set the off-diagonal entries to zero -> {{6+3d=0,\; 10+5d=0 => d=-2}}
S6. [calc] Evaluate the common diagonal entry at \(d=-2\) -> <<15+(-2)^2=19>>
S7. [symbolic] Since \(A^2=19I\), substitute into \(I=kA^2\) -> {{I=k(19I) => k=1/19}}
S8. [derive] Therefore the ordered pair is \((d,k)=(-2,1/19)\).

[Check]

[Answer]
\boxed{(-2,\frac{1}{19})}

The goal is to eliminate the parameters and write the plane as Ax + By + Cz + D = 0 with integer coefficients normalized as required. S4. [symbolic] Multiply by -1 to make the x-coefficient positive -> {{(-2,0,-1) * (-1) => (2,0,1)}}
S5. [derive] Using normal vector (2,0,1) and point (1,2,3), the plane is 2(x-1) + 0(y-2) + 1(z-3) = 0.
S6. [symbolic] Simplify the equation -> {{2(x-1) + 0(y-2) + 1(z-3) = 0 => 2x+z-5=0}}

[Overview]
This is a trigonometric equation problem. The goal is to find sin 2x. The key idea is to set p = sin x + cos x and q = sin x cos x, express the given equation in p and q, and use q = (p^2 - 1)/2.

[Plan]
P1. Define p = sin x + cos x and q = sin x cos x.
P2. Express all six terms in the given equation using p and q.
P3. Use the identity p^2 = 1 + 2q to eliminate q.
P4. Solve the resulting equation for p, rejecting values that make q zero or violate |p| <= sqrt(2).
P5. Compute sin 2x = 2q = p^2 - 1.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let s = sin x and c = cos x, and set p = s + c and q = sc. The original expression is defined only when sc != 0.
S2. [derive] Since s^2 + c^2 = 1, we have p^2 = (s+c)^2 = 1 + 2q, so q = (p^2 - 1)/2.
S3. [symbolic] Express the reciprocal trigonometric terms in p and q -> {{tan x + cot x + sec x + csc x = 1/q + p/q}}
S4. [derive] The given equation becomes p + (1+p)/q = 7.
S5. [symbolic] Multiply by q and rearrange using q = (p^2 - 1)/2 -> {{p + (1+p)/q = 7 => p^3 - 7p^2 + p + 9 = 0}}
S6. [symbolic] Factor the polynomial -> {{p^3 - 7p^2 + p + 9 = (p+1)(p^2-8p+9)}}
S7. [derive] If p = -1, then q = (p^2 - 1)/2 = 0, which is impossible because q = sin x cos x != 0. Thus p^2 - 8p + 9 = 0.
S8. [derive] The roots are p = 4 plus or minus sqrt(7). Since p = sin x + cos x must satisfy |p| <= sqrt(2), only p = 4 - sqrt(7) is possible.
S9. [symbolic] Compute sin 2x = 2sc = 2q = p^2 - 1 and use p^2 = 8p - 9 -> {{sin 2x = p^2 - 1 = 8p - 10 = 22 - 8sqrt(7)}}

[Check]
V1. For p = 4 - sqrt(7), p is approximately 1.354, which lies in [-sqrt(2), sqrt(2)], and q = (p^2 - 1)/2 is positive, so s and c are nonzero.
V2. Substituting p = 4 - sqrt(7) into p + (1+p)/q = 7 with q = (p^2 - 1)/2 is consistent with the derived polynomial equation.

[Answer]
\boxed{22 - 8\sqrt{7}}

[Overview]
This is a complex-plane inversion and area problem. The goal is to find the area of the image under w=1/z of the exterior of a regular hexagon. The key idea is that each exterior side half-plane maps to a disk, so S is the union of six congruent disks.

[Plan]
P1. Determine the inradius and side normals of the hexagon.
P2. Express the exterior as a union of six side-exterior half-planes.
P3. Apply the inversion w=1/z to map each half-plane to a disk.
P4. Identify the centers and radius of the six image disks.
P5. Compute the area of their union using polar coordinates and symmetry.
P6. Check the result with geometric bounds and boundary intersections.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let h be the distance from the center to any side. Since opposite sides are 1 unit apart, h=1/2. Let theta_k=k*pi/3, k=0,1,...,5, be the outward normal angles. The hexagon is defined by n_k dot z <= h for all k, where n_k=(cos(theta_k),sin(theta_k)).
S2. [derive] The exterior R is the union over k of the half-planes n_k dot z > h. Write w=1/z=u+iv. For a normal angle theta, the condition Re(z*exp(-i*theta))>h becomes u*cos(theta)-v*sin(theta)>h(u^2+v^2).
S3. [symbolic] Complete the square in the inequality -> {{u*cos(theta)-v*sin(theta) > h(u^2+v^2) => (u-cos(theta)/(2h))^2 + (v+sin(theta)/(2h))^2 < 1/(4h^2)}}.
S4. [calc] Since h=1/2, each image disk has radius 1 and center distance 1 from the origin -> <<1/(2*(1/2))=1>>.
S5. [theorem] Inversion is one-to-one on the punctured complex plane, so S is the union of these six unit disks, and boundary choices do not affect area.
S6. [setup] The six disk centers have angles -theta_k, so they form a regular hexagon of circumradius 1. By 60-degree symmetry, use polar coordinates w=r(cos(phi)+i*sin(phi)) for -pi/6 <= phi <= pi/6, where the nearest center has angle 0.
S7. [derive] Along the ray at angle phi, a unit disk centered at angle alpha contains points with 0<r<2*cos(phi-alpha) when the cosine is positive. The union extends to the nearest center, giving r_max=2*cos(phi) on this sector.
S8. [symbolic] Use polar area and sixfold symmetry -> {{Area = 6*(1/2)*int_{-pi/6}^{pi/6}(2*cos(phi))^2 dphi => Area = 12*int_{-pi/6}^{pi/6} cos^2(phi) dphi}}.
S9. [calc] Evaluate the integral -> <<12*(pi/6+sqrt(3)/4)=2*pi+3*sqrt(3)>>.

[Check]
V1. The value 2*pi+3*sqrt(3) is approximately 11.48, which is positive and less than the area 4*pi of the disk of radius 2 containing the union.
V2. At phi=pi/6, the radial distance is 2*cos(pi/6)=sqrt(3), which matches the outer intersection point of adjacent unit disks and confirms the sector boundaries join consistently.

[Answer]
\boxed{2\pi+3\sqrt{3}}

This is a polynomial divisibility problem involving cyclotomic factors. The goal is to find the smallest positive integer k such that the given polynomial divides z^k - 1. The key idea is to factor the polynomial into cyclotomic polynomials and take the least common multiple of the corresponding root orders.

[Plan]
P1. Factor the given polynomial into cyclotomic factors.
P2. Identify the root orders forced by those cyclotomic factors.
P3. Translate divisibility into divisibility conditions on k.
P4. Compute the least common multiple of the required orders.
P5. Verify that this value of k works and is minimal.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let P(z)=z^10+z^9+z^6+z^5+z^4+z+1. We seek the least positive k such that P(z) divides z^k-1.
S2. [derive] For a primitive 7th root rho, we have rho^7=1 and 1+rho+rho^2+rho^3+rho^4+rho^5+rho^6=0. Reducing the exponents of P(rho) modulo 7 gives all residues from 0 to 6 exactly once, so P(rho)=0. Hence Phi_7(z)=z^6+z^5+z^4+z^3+z^2+z+1 divides P(z).
S3. [symbolic] Divide P(z) by Phi_7(z) -> {{P(z)/(z^6+z^5+z^4+z^3+z^2+z+1) => z^4-z^2+1}}
S4. [theorem] z^k-1 equals the product of Phi_d(z) over all positive divisors d of k, and Phi_m(z) divides z^k-1 exactly when m divides k.
S5. [derive] The factorization is P(z)=Phi_7(z)Phi_12(z), because z^4-z^2+1=Phi_12(z). Therefore P(z) divides z^k-1 if and only if 7 divides k and 12 divides k.
S6. [calc] Least common multiple -> <<lcm(7,12)=84>>.
S7. [derive] The smallest positive integer satisfying both divisibility conditions is therefore k=84.

[Check]
V1. Since 7 and 12 divide 84, both Phi_7(z) and Phi_12(z) divide z^84-1, so P(z) divides z^84-1.
V2. If P(z) divides z^k-1, then both Phi_7(z) and Phi_12(z) must divide z^k-1, forcing 7 divides k and 12 divides k. Thus k must be at least lcm(7,12)=84.
V3. The factorization expands directly to P(z), confirming that the required factor orders are exactly 7 and 12.

[Answer]
\boxed{84}

S4. [derive] Since 2 sin(1/2) > 0, the inequality a_n < 0 is equivalent to cos(n+1/2) > cos(1/2).

[Plan]

P2. Use odd symmetry to reduce the count to positive roots plus the root at zero.

S2. [derive] For x > 0, the equation requires sin x > 0, so x must lie in intervals (2k*pi, (2k+1)*pi), k >= 0. Because x <= 100 and 32*pi > 100, only k = 0, 1, ..., 15 can contribute positive roots.

S4. [derive] For each k = 1, ..., 15, set a = 2k*pi, m = (2k + 1/2)*pi, b = (2k + 1)*pi. We have f(a) < 0 and f(b) < 0. Also m < 100, so f(m) = 1 - m/100 > 0. Using f'(x) = cos x - 0.01, the function has exactly one zero on (a, m) and exactly one zero on (m, b). Hence each interval k = 1, ..., 15 contributes two positive roots.

S5. [calc] Count the positive roots: <<1+2*15=31>>.

S6. [calc] Use symmetry and include x = 0 for the total number of real roots: <<31+31+1=63>>.

S1. [setup] Let the shaded area be the polygon area minus the areas of the two circle portions inside the polygon.
S2. [calc] The L-shaped polygon is a 12-by-4 rectangle minus a 4-by-2 notch, so its area is <<12*4-4*2=40>>.
S3. [derive] The smaller circle has radius 2 and center (2,-2), which lies on the bottom edge of its vertical strip. Only its upper semicircle lies inside the polygon.

[Check]

[Overview]
This is a tiling and minimization problem. The goal is to find the smallest number of 2-by-3 rectangles that can cover a square exactly. The key idea is to relate the number of rectangles to the square's side length by area, then use the square boundary to force the side length to be an integer.

[Plan]
P1. Let n be the number of rectangles and s be the square side length.
P2. Use the area equation from the total area of the rectangles and the square.
P3. Show that s must be an integer by examining how rectangle sides tile the square boundary.
P4. Determine the smallest possible integer s that makes the area equation valid.
P5. Construct an explicit tiling for that smallest case.
P6. Verify minimality and exact coverage.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let n be the positive number of 2-by-3 rectangles and let s be the side length of the square. Each rectangle has area 2*3=6, so the total area equation is s^2=6n.
S2. [theorem] Along each side of the square, the boundary is covered by full rectangle sides of length 2 or 3. Therefore each side length s is a sum of 2s and 3s, so s must be an integer.
S3. [derive] Since s is an integer and s^2=6n, the number s^2 must be divisible by 6. Divisibility by 2 and by 3 forces s to be divisible by 2 and by 3, hence s must be divisible by 6.
S4. [calc] The smallest positive integer side length divisible by 6 is s=6, giving the number of rectangles <<6^2/6=6>>.
S5. [derive] Since s must be a positive multiple of 6, we have s>=6. Hence n=s^2/6>=36/6=6. So fewer than 6 rectangles are impossible.
S6. [setup] A 6-by-6 square can be tiled exactly: divide it into three horizontal strips each measuring 6 by 2, and divide each strip into two 3-by-2 rectangles. These are rotated 2-by-3 rectangles, and the total count is 3*2=6.

[Check]
V1. Area check: six 2-by-3 rectangles have total area 6*6=36, matching a 6-by-6 square.
V2. Construction check: three 6-by-2 strips each split into two 3-by-2 rectangles cover the square with no gaps or overlaps.
V3. Minimality check: any valid integer side length must be divisible by 6, so s>=6 and therefore n>=6.

[Answer]
\boxed{6}

S1. [setup] Let a power of 2 be 2^n with n a nonnegative integer, and let a power of 8 be 8^k = 2^(3k).

S8. [derive] Thus the powers of 8 below 10^6 correspond to k = 0, 1, ..., 6.
S9. [calc] The number of such powers of 8 is -> <<6-0+1=7>>
S10. [calc] Subtract the excluded powers -> <<20-7=13>>

The key idea is that in a 30-60-90 triangle, the hypotenuse and longer leg have ratio \(2:\sqrt{3}\), so moving from one triangle to the adjacent smaller triangle multiplies the hypotenuse by \(\sqrt{3}/2\).

[Plan]

[Solution]
S1. [setup] The diagram shows four 30-60-90 triangles. Let the largest hypotenuse be \(8\) cm. In a 30-60-90 triangle, the longer leg equals \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) times the hypotenuse.
S2. [derive] Since the hypotenuse of each smaller triangle is the longer leg of the adjacent larger triangle, moving one triangle smaller multiplies the hypotenuse by \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).
S3. [calc] Moving three times from the largest hypotenuse to the smallest hypotenuse gives the smallest hypotenuse as <<8*(sqrt(3)/2)^3=3*sqrt(3)>>.
S4. [calc] The longer leg of the smallest triangle is the hypotenuse times \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\), so it equals <<(3*sqrt(3))*(sqrt(3)/2)=9/2>>.

[Overview]
This is a planar area problem on the simplex x+y+z=1. The goal is the normalized area of points satisfying exactly two of the three coordinate lower bounds. The key idea is that the thresholds 1/2, 1/3, and 1/6 sum to 1, so all three inequalities can hold simultaneously only at one point, which has area zero; hence the desired area is the sum of the three pairwise intersection areas.

[Plan]
P1. Project the simplex to the xy-plane using z=1-x-y and identify the triangular domain.
P2. Show that the triple-overlap region has area zero.
P3. Compute the area of each of the three pairwise intersections.
P4. Add the pairwise areas and divide by the area of the whole domain.
P5. Verify the result with a simple sanity check.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Use coordinates x and y, with z=1-x-y. The projected domain is D = {(x,y): x>=0, y>=0, x+y<=1}, whose area is 1/2. Let A be x>=1/2, B be y>=1/3, and C be z>=1/6. Since projection changes all areas by the same constant factor, area ratios may be computed in D.
S2. [derive] If A, B, and C are all true, then x+y+z >= 1/2+1/3+1/6 = 1. Since x+y+z=1, equality forces (x,y,z) = (1/2,1/3,1/6), a single point. Thus the triple overlap has area zero, and the desired area equals the sum of the areas of A and B, A and C, and B and C, up to zero-area overlap.
S3. [calc] The region where A and B hold has x>=1/2, y>=1/3, x+y<=1. This is a right triangle with legs 1/6 and 1/6, so its area is <<(1/2)*(1/6)*(1/6)=1/72>>.
S4. [calc] The region where A and C hold has x>=1/2 and z>=1/6, so y<=5/6-x and y>=0. This is a right triangle with legs 1/3 and 1/3, so its area is <<(1/2)*(1/3)*(1/3)=1/18>>.
S5. [calc] The region where B and C hold has y>=1/3 and z>=1/6, so x<=5/6-y and x>=0. This is a right triangle with legs 1/2 and 1/2, so its area is <<(1/2)*(1/2)*(1/2)=1/8>>.
S6. [calc] Add the three pairwise areas: <<1/72+1/18+1/8=7/36>>.
S7. [calc] Divide by the area of D: <<(7/36)/(1/2)=7/18>>.

[Check]
V1. The thresholds sum to 1, so the triple overlap is only the single point (1/2,1/3,1/6), which has area zero; this confirms that no positive area is double-counted.
V2. The resulting ratio is between 0 and 1: <<0 < 7/18 < 1>>.

[Answer]
\boxed{\frac{7}{18}}

solution:
[Overview]
This is a trigonometric equation counting problem. The goal is to count solutions of tan x = tan(tan x) on a closed interval. The key idea is to set y = tan x, reducing the equation to y = tan y, then count how many such y values lie in [0, 942].

[Plan]
P1. Substitute y = tan x and rewrite the equation.
P2. Use monotonicity of tan x on the given interval to match each y value with exactly one x value.
P3. Analyze the equation y = tan y on intervals between consecutive asymptotes.
P4. Count the positive y solutions up to 942 and include the zero solution.
P5. Convert the count of y solutions back to x solutions.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let y = tan x. Since 0 <= x <= arctan 942 and arctan 942 < pi/2, the map x -> y = tan x is one-to-one from [0, arctan 942] onto [0, 942].
S2. [derive] Under y = tan x, the original equation tan x = tan(tan x) becomes y = tan y. Thus each solution y in [0, 942] gives exactly one solution x = arctan y.
S3. [theorem] On each interval (n pi - pi/2, n pi + pi/2), the function tan y is strictly increasing, so tan y = y has at most one solution there.
S4. [case] The value y = 0 is a solution. For 0 < y < pi/2, the given fact tan y > y rules out positive solutions in (0, pi/2).
S5. [derive] For each integer n >= 1, on (n pi, n pi + pi/2), tan y increases from 0 to infinity. Since tan(n pi) = 0 < n pi and tan y tends to infinity before n pi + pi/2, there is exactly one solution of tan y = y in (n pi, n pi + pi/2). There are no positive solutions where tan y < 0.
S6. [derive] The interval for n = 299 is (299 pi, 299 pi + pi/2). Its right endpoint is 299 pi + pi/2 = 940.906999750143... < 942, so its unique root lies below 942. The next interval starts at 300 pi = 942.477796076938... > 942, so it contributes no root in [0, 942].
S7. [derive] Therefore the positive solutions y correspond exactly to n = 1, 2, ..., 299, giving 299 positive solutions. Including y = 0 gives 300 solutions y in [0, 942].
S8. [derive] Since each such y gives exactly one x = arctan y in the original interval, the number of x solutions is also 300.

[Check]
V1. The endpoint arctan 942 is less than pi/2, so tan is one-to-one on the whole x interval and no solution is duplicated.
V2. The last possible positive root lies in (299 pi, 299 pi + pi/2), entirely below 942, while the next interval begins after 942, so no solution is missed.

[Answer]
\boxed{300}
